title: Dark Matter
subtitle: The invisible majority
yt_title: 85% of All Matter Is Invisible 🌑 | Ep. 86 #shorts
description:
Episode 86 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌑
Dark matter: Fritz Zwicky noticed in 1933 that galaxy clusters move too fast, and Vera Rubin showed in the 1970s that galaxies spin too fast. About 85% of all matter seems to be invisible. Nobody knows what it is.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 87: Next stop, a ring of fire in the sky. The annular solar eclipse of February 6.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

segments.text: Episode eighty-six. Next stop... dark matter.
In nineteen thirty-three, astronomer Fritz Zwicky studied a cluster of galaxies, and noticed they were moving way too fast.
segments.headline: Too fast, 1933

segments.text: With only the matter we could see, their gravity should not have been strong enough to hold them together.
segments.headline: Missing gravity

segments.text: In the nineteen seventies, astronomer Vera Rubin measured how galaxies spin. The outer stars moved just as fast as the inner ones.
segments.headline: Vera Rubin's discovery

segments.text: They should have flown away. Something invisible was holding them in. Astronomers called it dark matter.
segments.headline: Dark matter

segments.text: Today we think about eighty-five percent of all the matter in the universe is dark matter.
It doesn't shine, reflect or block light. We only see its gravity, bending the light of distant galaxies.
segments.headline: Only its gravity

segments.text: Scientists have built detectors deep underground to catch dark matter particles. So far, nothing.
segments.headline: The hunt continues

segments.text: The new Vera Rubin Observatory, named after her, will map dark matter across billions of galaxies.
segments.headline: Rubin will map it

segments.text: Tomorrow, a ring of fire is coming to the sky. Next stop: the annular eclipse. Follow, so you don't miss episode eighty-seven.
